_comment: The report shown by 'See sample report'. Hand-written for a fictional account, not generated: lib/mock.js exists for tests and says 'Mock reading for agreeableness' on purpose, which is right for a fixture and wrong for a shop window. Shaped to PROFILE_SCHEMA in lib/prompts.js, and a check holds it there. Deliberately not a flattering read — a sample that only praises would misrepresent what the model actually returns.

confidence.rationale: Four years of steady, well-dated posting, and captions long enough to read tone from rather than guess at — that is about as much as an export gives. Beliefs and attachment are the thinner end: you write warmly but rarely about yourself, so those two lean on indirect evidence while everything above them rests on behaviour that repeats.

essence.why: You do the thing nobody assigned you and you do it quietly, which is the resemblance — not the sword. Forty-seven posts naming a deadline and forty-one closing it out, four years of it, and the wins written as ours rather than mine. The comparison earns itself on what is missing: no post in four years says the load was heavy, and Mulan is the same kind of competent that would rather absorb the cost than be seen carrying it.

summary:
You come across as an organiser with a warm centre. High conscientiousness, high agreeableness, and moderate extraversion in a way that surprises people who assume you are an extrovert because you are always at the thing. You post in clusters around events you arranged, then go quiet for a fortnight. That is not inconsistency; it is recovery.

What you value shows up in what you do rather than what you say. Four years of captions and barely a sentence about yourself that is not attached to somebody else's news. Generous with attention, sparing with disclosure — which reads as modesty and works as a wall.

At work the same shape holds. You notice what has not been assigned and do it, which makes you indispensable and, on this evidence, slightly under-credited.

cardHighlights: Like her, you would rather absorb the cost than be seen carrying it: four years of posts, and not one says the load was heavy. When it goes well, the win is written as ours rather than mine, the same quiet competence that keeps the credit pointed away from you. Underneath, you read as an organiser with a warm centre, always at the thing and then gone quiet to recover rather than out of inconsistency. What you value shows in what you do rather than what you say, because your captions barely mention you without attaching the news to somebody else.

openness.reading: Curious inside familiar territory rather than restless for new. The same three trailheads for four years, but the books and routes within them keep changing.
evidence: Captions reference 14 distinct book titles across 2022–2025, none repeated
Location tags cluster on three parks, 78% of all tagged posts

conscientiousness.reading: The strongest signal here. You post plans before they happen and follow through after, and the gap between the two is small.
evidence: 47 posts naming a specific date or deadline, 41 followed by a completion post
Weekly posting variance is low — a steady 2–3 per week for 30 of 48 months

extraversion.reading: Social in bursts, solitary in between — not the same as being an extrovert. You enjoy people and appear to need recovering from them.
evidence: Group posts cluster into 9 bursts of 3–5 days, each followed by a 10+ day gap
You publish far less than you consume: 312 posts against 8,400 likes

agreeableness.reading: Almost every comment you write is about somebody else's news. You disagree rarely, and soften it first when you do.
evidence: 84% of your comments appear on other people's posts, not replies on your own
Recurring openers: 'so proud of', 'this is so you', 'let me know if'

neuroticism.reading: Steadier than most, with a tell: posting drops sharply for a week or two after your busiest stretches. A battery you deplete and refill on schedule.
evidence: Caption length drops ~40% during the quiet stretches after event clusters
Two multi-week gaps follow the account's two busiest months

letters.why: You are the named organiser in most of the forty-odd event clusters this account is built around, and the posting spikes on their dates rather than trailing them — you are making the occasion, not attending it. Thirty-one distinct people appear in your comments, which is a genuinely wide circle rather than a handful. Against that, six accounts absorb most of the engagement, every cluster is followed by roughly a fortnight of silence, and your messages run long and few rather than short and many — all three are textbook introversion, and the last is the one this data most often misreads. What tips it to E is that the organising is outward-facing and four years repeated, not that the volume is high; at an extraversion score of 52 this is as close as an axis gets.
letters.inPractice: You will happily host the thing and be the first to leave it.

letters.why: Of the fifty sampled captions, twenty-two go past recording the event to say what it meant — a comparison, a pattern, or a 'which is basically what happened last year'. That is well above what the format asks for, since a caption's job here is to describe the picture. Your searches lean the same way, running more 'why does' than 'how to' across the sampled term list. The tempering is real though: the other twenty-eight captions are precise concrete description — places, dates, model names — and there is a sustained run of practical how-to searching across the last eighteen months. Instagram rewards exactly that specificity, so it reads closer to the platform's baseline than to a preference, which is why it moderates the letter rather than overturning it.
letters.inPractice: You are quick to see where something is going, and occasionally ahead of the evidence.

letters.why: Nine captions across the four years show a decision being made, and in almost all of them the thing that settles it is the effect on somebody — including the purely logistical ones. Your most-liked accounts are individuals rather than subjects by roughly three to one, an appetite that is people-shaped rather than topic-shaped. The warm comment history is deliberately not counted here: congratulation is what a comment box is for and every account looks kind by that measure. What does count against the letter is that the forty-seven deadline posts are tracked on delivery rather than on who was affected, and your captions about other people's work assess it about as often as they celebrate it — a real thinking streak, and enough to keep this off clear.
letters.inPractice: You will pick the option that keeps everyone comfortable over the one that is simply correct.

letters.why: Forty-seven posts name a deadline and forty-one of them close it out, a follow-through rate most accounts never show. Weekly posting variance is low enough to be predictable across thirty of forty-eight months, and saved things get returned to rather than accumulating unread. The nearest thing to a contrary reading is that the clusters themselves are bursty rather than evenly paced — but they burst around scheduled events, which is planning rather than spontaneity. This is the one axis here the data leaves little room to argue with, so it is clear rather than moderate.
letters.inPractice: Uncertainty costs you more energy than work does.

mbti.caveat: MBTI is popular rather than validated, and this one is inferred indirectly from behaviour rather than from any questionnaire. Treat the E as the softest of the four.

posting.headline: Steady, planned, event-shaped
posting.detail: Two to three posts a week, clustered around things you organised. Carousels outnumber single images two to one — you post the occasion, not the best frame from it.

rhythm.headline: Early mornings, weekend-weighted
rhythm.detail: 61% of posts go up between 5am and 8am, and Saturday is your busiest day by a distance. Almost nothing after 9pm.

trajectory.headline: Tapering, and deliberately
trajectory.detail: Posting peaked in 2023 and has fallen about 35% since, while commenting stayed flat. You have not lost interest in the people, only in broadcasting.

diet.headline: Narrow, warm, mostly people you already know
diet.detail: 8,400 likes against 312 posts — you read about twenty-seven times more than you publish. The concentration is the finding: roughly half those likes land on twelve accounts, and ten of the twelve are people you know personally. You follow 634 accounts and have engaged with 41 of them in the past year, so the other 593 are a subscription you are still paying for and no longer reading. Set against that, 190 saved posts — about 140 of them recipes and training plans — while your captions show the same three trailheads and the same twelve-week block four years running.

interests.name: Distance running
interests.detail: Not a phase — four consecutive years of training blocks with the same structure, and the vocabulary of someone who has read about it as well as done it.
interests.evidence: 63 posts tagged at three trailheads, recurring 'week n of 12' captions

interests.name: Cooking for people
interests.detail: Almost always for others and almost never a photograph of the finished plate alone — the table is in shot.
interests.evidence: 41 posts, 38 of which include other people or multiple place settings

interests.name: Reading
interests.detail: Wide rather than deep, and skewed towards non-fiction about how things work.
interests.evidence: 14 distinct titles named in captions, none repeated

interests.name: Live music
interests.detail: Concentrated in summer and almost entirely with the same group.

values.detail: You treat a commitment as binding in a way most accounts do not show. The follow-through rate on things you announce is the clearest number in this report.
values.evidence: 41 of 47 announced plans have a matching completion post

values.detail: You care how a thing is done, not only that it got done — visible in the way you describe other people's work as much as your own.
values.evidence: Comments frequently name a specific detail rather than praising generally

values.detail: Nearly everything you publish is about a group rather than an individual, yours included.
values.evidence: 71% of posts contain more than one person

scores.line: You plan your own way but rarely for yourself alone – most of your independent choices are about how to run something for others.
New things appear, but as occasions to organise rather than thrills to chase.
Pleasure shows up as shared meals and gigs, almost never as something you do just for you.
Finishing is visible everywhere – deadlines named and closed, races entered and run.
Nothing in four years reaches for status or control; you lead by doing the work, not by holding the title.
Routines, plans made weeks ahead, and the same close circle for years.
You keep the peace and rarely post anything that would upset anyone.
Birthdays and rituals matter to you as gatherings, less as heritage.
Almost everything you publish is about looking after your own people – the clearest signal in the report.
Some causes and charity runs, but the care is mostly local rather than global.

motivators.reading: Your strongest pull is care for the people close to you, backed by achievement: you want things done well, and done for them. The tension is between that care and your own needs – power and enjoyment sit at the bottom, which reads less like modesty than like a life arranged around other people's plans.

strengths.title: You remember
strengths.detail: Dates, follow-ups, the thing someone was nervous about last month. Your comments return to other people's earlier posts with a specificity that is hard to fake and rare to find.

strengths.title: Low-drama by default
strengths.detail: Four years without a single public disagreement is not avoidance on this evidence — it reads as someone who handles friction privately and promptly.

weaknesses.title: You do not ask
weaknesses.detail: There is almost no example here of you requesting anything for yourself. In a close relationship that becomes a problem for the other person, who is left guessing and eventually gets it wrong.

weaknesses.title: Score-keeping in silence
weaknesses.detail: The same giving-first pattern: generous in the moment, quietly tallying, and inclined to feel unmet without ever having stated the need. Nothing here shows it blowing up, but the ingredients are visible.

receiving.why: The posts you write most warmly about are unhurried and undivided — a long walk, a slow dinner, nowhere to be afterwards.
receiving.inPractice: An evening cleared for you lands harder than anything bought for you.

receiving.why: The rare posts where you quote something someone said about you are kept and repeated.
receiving.inPractice: Specific beats effusive — name the thing you noticed.

giving.why: Your account is a four-year record of doing things for people: the lifts, the bookings, the collecting, the cooking.
giving.inPractice: You show love by removing a problem, often before it is mentioned.

loveLanguages.caveat: Love languages are a popular framework rather than a validated instrument. Read these as a decent guess at what you reach for, not a diagnosis.

strengths.title: Finishes things
strengths.detail: The follow-through rate visible in this account is the trait most organisations are shortest of. You close what you open.

strengths.title: Holds the group together
strengths.detail: You reliably do the unassigned work that keeps a team functioning — the scheduling, the chasing, the remembering.

weaknesses.title: Under-claims
weaknesses.detail: You narrate collective wins and almost never individual ones. On this evidence you are more likely to be under-credited than over-credited, and unlikely to correct it.

weaknesses.title: Absorbs the overflow
weaknesses.detail: Work that has no owner appears to become yours by default. That is why you are valuable and why you are probably tired.

career.workStyle: Plans in blocks, announces the plan, delivers to it. High standards applied quietly rather than argued for.
career.watchOuts: Somewhere with no natural end to the work, or a culture where credit goes to whoever claims it loudest.

bonus.harsh:
You have saved about 140 recipes and training plans over four years, and your own captions show the same three trailheads and the same twelve-week block on repeat every one of those years. That folder is not a plan, it is a shrine. Meanwhile the actual pattern here is beautifully consistent: you do things for people without being asked, and you have never once, in four years of posts, asked anyone for anything back. That is not generosity running unchecked, it is a ledger you have decided not to show anyone — which is why 'quietly tallying' shows up in your own relationship read a page ago, and why nobody around you has learned to reciprocate, because you have never given them the information required to try.

And the tell is the thing that is not here at all: forty-one posts closing out a plan, zero admitting the plan was heavy. An organiser who never once says the load is a lot is not calm, they are unwilling to find out what happens if they put it down for a week and see who notices.
bonus.advice: Cook one of the hundred and forty recipes instead of saving a hundred and forty-first — the gap between the folder and the plate is the actual finding, not the folder. Unfollow the five hundred and ninety-three accounts you have not engaged with in a year; a subscription you are not reading is not community, it is guilt with a notification badge. And say the specific thing out loud to one specific person: not 'I'm fine', the actual sentence — 'I need you to plan the next one' or 'I noticed you didn't ask how my week was' — because a need that is never stated is a need nobody can meet, and you already know that, you just have not tried saying it where it could be heard.

buildOn.title: Your follow-through
buildOn.detail: You close what you open, which most people and most teams are short of. Use it deliberately: pick the commitments you take on rather than inheriting them.

buildOn.title: The circle you keep
buildOn.detail: The same close group for years is rare and worth protecting. It is also where you could start being looked after as well as looking after.

develop.title: Let the credit land
develop.detail: You narrate collective wins and almost never your own part in them, so the people who rely on you most may not know how much you carry. Under pressure your reliability tips into absorbing everyone's overflow.
earlySigns: Saying yes before checking your calendar
Sending every reminder in the group chat
develop.counterMove: Before taking on the next unassigned job, name who else could do it and ask them first.

actions.step: When the next thing you organised comes off, write one line that says you organised it.
Hand one recurring job – the booking, the reminders – to someone else and leave it with them.

develop.reflect: Whose job are you doing that nobody asked you to do – and what would happen if you stopped?

develop.title: Say the heavy part out loud
develop.detail: Nothing in your writing admits a hard week, which keeps people at a warm distance and leaves you carrying the cost alone. Under strain your warmth turns into keeping the peace at your own expense.
earlySigns: Agreeing in the moment and resenting it later
Going quiet with one person while staying warm with everyone else
develop.counterMove: Raise the small thing within a day, in one sentence, while it is still small.

actions.step: Tell one person in your inner circle one thing that has been hard this month, without fixing it for them.

develop.reflect: Who knows how you are actually doing right now?

lifeTrajectory.reading: Four years of the same few commitments, kept: the same running routes, the same friends, the same hosting rhythm. Nothing here shows drift or a stretch where things came loose.
evidence: Same three trailheads every spring, 2021–2025
About nine hosted events a year, every year

outlook.reading: Your captions are warm about other people and almost silent about yourself, so there is little direct evidence of how you feel about where you are. What there is reads as content rather than restless.
evidence: 3 of 60 sampled captions about your own feelings

socialConnection.reading: Wide and active: comments on 64 different people's posts in a year, and messages spread across many threads rather than one or two. The connection runs mostly outward, from you to them.
evidence: Comments on 64 different people's posts in a year
Messages across 38 active conversations

cognitiveLoad.reading: Plans, reminders and follow-ups for other people make up a large share of what you write, often late in the evening. It reads as a lot being carried, by you, with no post saying so.
evidence: Group plans in 38 of 60 sampled captions
A third of messages sent after 10pm in event weeks

meaning.reading: What you do lines up with what you value: care for your people and getting things done show up in the same posts. The meaning is real; it is just rarely about you.
evidence: 47 posts naming a deadline, 41 closing one out

rhythmAndActivity.reading: Regular runs most weeks, then a fortnight of near-silence after each busy stretch. The rhythm is healthy on average and uneven up close.
evidence: Typical quiet stretch after an event: 13 days
Running posts in 40 of 52 weeks

wellness.overall: A steady, well-connected life with one clear pressure point: the load you carry for other people, carried quietly and late. Social connection is your strongest dimension; cognitive load is the one worth watching first.

suggestions.title: Protect the recovery fortnight
suggestions.detail: After a big event, keep the quiet stretch on purpose rather than filling it with the next plan.

attachment.style: Leans secure, with a self-reliant streak
attachment.styleTone: Steady, warm and dependable – people can count on you, and you rarely make closeness feel like hard work.
attachment.why: Steady reply times, no bursts of messages after a silence, and warmth spread across many people point to secure. Avoidant was considered and set aside: you seek people out constantly. What keeps it from plain secure is how rarely you lean on anyone yourself.
attachment.conflict: You smooth friction over in the moment and raise it later, in private, if at all – you would rather absorb a small annoyance than turn it into a conversation. It keeps things calm, and it means the people close to you rarely learn what bothered you until you have already made up your mind about it. Saying the small thing early, while it is still small, costs you less than you expect.
derivedFrom: Replies within the hour in 70% of threads
No message bursts after a gap in four years
3 of 60 captions about your own feelings

implications.title: Easy to be close to
implications.detail: You make plans, show up and follow through, so the people around you feel safe with you.

implications.title: Hard to look after
implications.detail: You give first and ask rarely, so partners can feel they never get the chance to care for you back.

attachment.caveat: Attachment style cannot be read reliably from social-media data. Treat this as an informed guess.

needs.title: Someone who notices without being told
needs.detail: You will not ask, so you do best with a partner who picks up on a quiet week and acts on it.

needs.title: Unhurried time together
needs.detail: Your warmest posts are about long walks and slow dinners – a partner who values the same rhythm will feel like home.

carefulOf.title: A partner who lets you carry everything
carefulOf.detail: You will take on the planning by default; someone happy to let you will leave you quietly tired.

idealPartner.summary: You suit someone steady and attentive who shares the load without being asked and is comfortable with your quiet stretches. The risk is not conflict but imbalance – choose someone who gives back as readily as you give.

careerAssessment.situation: You appear to be in a role where you coordinate people and deadlines, formally or not, and are relied on more than you are recognised.

edge.headline: You finish what you start
edge.detail: Forty-one of forty-seven deadlines you posted about were closed out. Reliable follow-through is the trait most teams are shortest of, and you have it in quantity.
evidence: 47 posts naming a deadline, 41 closing one out
Same plans announced and delivered across four years

underused.headline: Your own name on the work
underused.detail: You write every win as "we". The record of what you personally delivered is there – you just never show it.

holdingBack.headline: Absorbing the unowned work
holdingBack.detail: Work without an owner becomes yours by default. It makes you indispensable and leaves less room for the work that would move you forward.

actions.title: Aim for a role that rewards follow-through
actions.detail: Operations, programme or project leadership – where finishing things is the job, not the extra.
